quests.question: The movie I watched last night was terrifying. What has happened to the relative clause in this sentence?
quests.hint: Try inserting 'that' or 'which' right after 'movie' - does the sentence still make the same sense? Then ask what role 'the movie' plays inside that added clause.
quests.explanation: 'I watched' already has its own subject ('I'), so 'the movie' is the object of 'watched.' Object relative pronouns like 'that' can be omitted, which is exactly what happened here - the full version would be 'The movie that I watched...'
options: There is no relative clause in this sentence at all.
The relative pronoun has been left out because the clause describes a subject.
The sentence is grammatically incorrect as written.
The relative pronoun has been left out because the clause describes an object.
quests.correctAnswer: The relative pronoun has been left out because the clause describes an object.

quests.question: Which sentence has its relative pronoun omitted?
quests.hint: Look for the sentence where a noun is directly followed by a subject and a verb, with no connecting word in between.
quests.explanation: In 'The dish I ordered arrived cold,' the object relative pronoun has been dropped entirely - 'I ordered' follows 'the dish' with no connector, which is only possible for object relative clauses.
options: The waiter who served us was very attentive.
The soup that I ordered was too salty.
The dish I ordered arrived cold.
The restaurant which we visited has closed.
quests.correctAnswer: The dish I ordered arrived cold.

quests.question: Which sentence means exactly the same thing as: 'The song that she recorded became a hit'?
quests.hint: Removing the pronoun should not remove any other information - check that both 'she' and 'recorded' are still there.
quests.explanation: 'The song she recorded became a hit' keeps the exact same meaning: 'that,' the object relative pronoun, is simply dropped, since 'the song' is the object of 'recorded' and 'she' remains the clause's subject.
options: The song recorded became a hit.
She recorded became a hit.
The song that recorded became a hit.
The song she recorded became a hit.
quests.correctAnswer: The song she recorded became a hit.

quests.question: Which sentence below is grammatically correct?
quests.hint: This clause needs its own subject - the gap itself must supply it here, so nothing can be left out.
quests.explanation: Because 'the man' is the subject of 'works' (there's no other candidate), the relative pronoun cannot be omitted - it must stay, and since he's a person and the subject, 'who' is correct.
options: The man works at the pharmacy is my neighbor.
The man who works at the pharmacy is my neighbor.
The man which works at the pharmacy is my neighbor.
The man whom works at the pharmacy is my neighbor.
quests.correctAnswer: The man who works at the pharmacy is my neighbor.
quests.grammarRule: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted

quests.question: Which version below is the grammatically correct one?
quests.hint: Check whether the clause already has its own subject elsewhere ('I') - if so, the object pronoun can safely disappear.
quests.explanation: 'I' is the subject of 'met,' so 'the man' is the object - an object relative pronoun here, so it can be dropped entirely, giving 'The man I met...'
options: The man met at the pharmacy is my neighbor.
The man whom met at the pharmacy is my neighbor.
The man which I met at the pharmacy is my neighbor.
The man I met at the pharmacy is my neighbor.
quests.correctAnswer: The man I met at the pharmacy is my neighbor.

quests.explanation: 'Sits' has no other subject, so the relative pronoun cannot be omitted here; 'who' must stay because 'the colleague' - a person - is the subject of 'sits.'

quests.question: Which sentence contains a grammatical error?
quests.hint: Check each clause: does it already have its own subject, or does the missing word need to supply one?
quests.explanation: In 'The friend called me last night lives abroad,' 'called me last night' has no subject of its own - 'the friend' must supply it, so the relative pronoun ('who') cannot be dropped. All the other sentences are object relative clauses, where omission is fine.
options: The friend called me last night lives abroad.

quests.question: The article ___ criticized the new policy sparked a huge backlash.
quests.hint: Check whether 'criticized' already has a subject somewhere else in the sentence.
quests.explanation: 'Criticized' has no other subject - 'the article' must supply it, so the relative pronoun cannot be dropped here. Since it's a thing acting as the subject, 'that' is required.
options: (no word needed)
that
who
whom
quests.correctAnswer: that
quests.grammarRule: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted

quests.question: Which version of this sentence is NOT grammatically acceptable?
quests.hint: Three of these are simply different valid ways to express the same object relative clause - only one breaks a basic rule.
quests.explanation: 'Whom' can only refer to people, never things, so 'The policy whom the senator criticized...' is ungrammatical. The other three are all acceptable: the object relative pronoun can be 'that,' 'which,' or simply omitted.
options: The policy that the senator criticized sparked a huge backlash.
The policy whom the senator criticized sparked a huge backlash.
The policy the senator criticized sparked a huge backlash.
The policy which the senator criticized sparked a huge backlash.
quests.correctAnswer: The policy whom the senator criticized sparked a huge backlash.

quests.question: Formal: 'This is the gift that my sister gave me.' Which casual rewrite keeps the same meaning and is grammatically correct?
quests.hint: Removing the connector shouldn't scramble the rest of the sentence - the subject and verb inside the clause should stay in their normal order.
quests.explanation: 'This is the gift my sister gave me' is the natural, casual version: the object relative pronoun 'that' is simply dropped, while 'my sister gave me' keeps its normal subject-verb-object order.
options: This is the gift gave me my sister.
This is the gift which gave me my sister.
This is the gift my sister gave me.
This is the gift my sister that gave me.
quests.correctAnswer: This is the gift my sister gave me.

quests.question: Casual: 'The guy I talked to seemed nice.' Which is the more formal, fully-written version?
quests.hint: Restoring the missing pronoun means adding back a word - and since the antecedent is a person in object position, only one option fits both criteria.
quests.explanation: 'Whom' is the formally correct object pronoun for a person; restoring it reproduces the same meaning as the casual, omitted version.
options: The guy talked to me seemed nice.
The guy whom I talked to seemed nice.
The guy which I talked to seemed nice.
The guy I talked to whom seemed nice.
quests.correctAnswer: The guy whom I talked to seemed nice.

quests.question: Which sentence best matches this meaning: 'I finally found my keys. I had lost my keys last week.'?
quests.hint: Check that the clause still has its subject and the correct verb tense, even without a connecting pronoun.
quests.explanation: 'I finally found the keys I had lost last week' correctly omits the object relative pronoun while keeping 'I' as the clause's subject and using the correct past perfect tense, 'had lost,' to show the losing happened before the finding.
options: I finally found the keys had lost last week.
I finally found the keys who had lost last week.
I finally found the keys I have lost last week.
I finally found the keys I had lost last week.
quests.correctAnswer: I finally found the keys I had lost last week.

quests.question: Which of these versions breaks a basic grammar rule?
quests.hint: Three of these express the same idea in different registers - only one breaks a basic grammar rule about what this pronoun can do.
quests.explanation: 'Whose' must be immediately followed by the noun it possesses (like 'whose car'); it cannot stand alone as a direct object the way 'whom,' 'who,' or an omitted pronoun can.
options: This is the man I met at the wedding.
This is the man whose I met at the wedding.
This is the man who I met at the wedding.
This is the man whom I met at the wedding.
quests.correctAnswer: This is the man whose I met at the wedding.

quests.question: This is the man ___ I met at the wedding. Which option would sound most natural if you were casually telling a friend this story out loud?
quests.hint: Think about how briefly people actually speak in casual storytelling - what's the shortest natural option?
quests.explanation: In casual spoken English, the object relative pronoun is very often dropped entirely - 'This is the man I met at the wedding' - making omission the most natural, casual choice, even more common than 'who.'
options: whom
(leave it out entirely)
whose
which
quests.correctAnswer: (leave it out entirely)

quests.question: In her formal email, she wrote: 'Please find attached the resume of the candidate ___ we interviewed last week.'

whose
whom
who

our trip
last night
beautifully
